items.title: 10.27 Winkler method, BOD and DO (numbered 10.27 as printed)

source_refs.note: Printed as 10.27 (10.23 to 10.26 absent) with Figure 10.12, pages 239-240. The exercise (pages 240-243) is not reproduced.

blocks.title: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)
blocks.text: BOD is the capacity of the organic matter in natural water to consume oxygen within a period of five days. Its value is the amount of oxygen consumed by the biological oxidation of dissolved organic matter in the sample, a reaction catalysed by microorganisms already present in the water. It is measured by the Winkler method from the oxygen concentration at the beginning and at the end of the five-day period, during which a sealed sample is kept in the dark at a constant 25 degrees C.

blocks.title: Dissolved oxygen (DO)
blocks.text: DO is the amount of oxygen dissolved in water, from the atmosphere or released by plants during photosynthesis in the water. Its concentration is between 5 and 8 mg per dm3; the minimum level should be 5 mg per dm3, and below this the water is taken to be polluted.
DO and BOD have an inverse relationship (Figure 10.12): as bacteria consume oxygen while decomposing organic matter, BOD increases and the dissolved oxygen level falls.

blocks.alt: Graph of concentration against direction of flow of river. Dissolved Oxygen (solid line) is high, falls suddenly to a minimum and then rises slowly back to a high level. BOD (dotted line) is low, rises steeply at the same point to a peak and then falls gradually, crossing the dissolved oxygen curve.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.12: Inverse relationship between BOD and DO (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.12 spells 'Disolved Oxygen'; the correct spelling is Dissolved Oxygen.

The Winkler method measures the dissolved oxygen in water samples. It is based on the oxidising property of the dissolved oxygen, which reacts with KI; the iodine formed is measured by titration with sodium thiosulfate using starch as indicator, which turns the solution dark blue to show the end point. The amount of iodine formed is proportional to the amount of dissolved oxygen in the solution.
